Never retrying side-effectful operations trades duplicate tickets for silently lost tickets on every transient blip — usually the worse failure mode for a support platform. The engineering answer is making the retry safe, not surrendering reliability to avoid duplication.

Shortening the timeout increases the number of ambiguous races: more first attempts get abandoned mid-flight while still completing server-side. It manufactures more of exactly the uncertainty that produces duplicates, based on a guess about server timing.
principle: retries plus side effects require idempotency, not luck
relatedConcept: Timeout-and-retry is safe only when operations are idempotent — idempotency keys let backends deduplicate repeated attempts of one logical action.
overallExplanation: A timed-out request may still have succeeded, so retrying side-effectful operations demands idempotency. Client-generated idempotency keys let the backend collapse duplicates while keeping timeouts and retries in place.

question: At a weather-data company, developers use Claude to draft substantial pull requests. A subtle unit-conversion bug — knots versus meters per second — shipped last week in an AI-drafted PR that was merged as soon as CI turned green, with no human reading the diff. What should the engineering lead change about the process?
options: Require the same human code review rigor for AI-drafted changes as for human ones — a green CI run is a necessary gate, but reviewers must still verify logic and domain correctness
Prohibit AI-drafted pull requests for numerical code, since unit handling is a class of logic that language models cannot contribute to safely
Add a second AI pass that reviews every AI-drafted PR, replacing human review with a cheaper automated judgment layer
Require developers to retype AI-drafted changes by hand before committing, so the code passes through a human's fingers even if not their judgment
optionExplanations: Correct. Code review discipline does not relax because a model wrote the diff — if anything, plausible-looking AI output warrants sharper scrutiny, since it reads confidently even when subtly wrong. CI proves the tests pass; it cannot prove the tests cover unit semantics nobody thought to assert.

A blanket ban discards real productivity over one process failure. The bug shipped because no human reviewed the diff, not because AI touched numerical code — properly reviewed AI-drafted changes to numerical code are as governable as any other contribution.

An AI reviewer can be a useful additional signal, but replacing human review outsources accountability to another fallible model — potentially sharing the same blind spot that produced the bug. Review exists to put responsible human judgment on the change before it ships.

Retyping is ritual, not review: transcription engages the fingers while the unit-conversion bug sails through unchanged. It adds toil without adding the missing ingredient, which is a human actually reasoning about the diff's correctness.
principle: AI-drafted code gets full human review — green CI is necessary, not sufficient
relatedConcept: Code review is an accountability mechanism: whoever merges owns the change, and AI authorship raises rather than lowers the bar for scrutiny.
overallExplanation: The defect was process, not provenance: an unreviewed diff shipped on a green build. AI-drafted changes require the same human review as any code, because CI validates only what the tests already assert.

question: A music-streaming service enriches track metadata with a TypeScript job. The developer made the function async, yet 5,000 Claude API calls still take hours: profiling shows each iteration of a for-of loop awaits its API call before the next begins. The API's rate limits have plenty of headroom. What is the correct fix?
options: Launch the calls concurrently — for example with Promise.all over batches or a bounded concurrency pool — instead of awaiting each request before starting the next
Move the loop into Node worker threads, since JavaScript's single-threaded event loop is what forces the API calls to run one at a time
Raise the HTTP client's timeout so each request has more time to complete, reducing the per-call overhead that accumulates across iterations
Convert the code to synchronous blocking calls, since async/await adds scheduling overhead that dominates in tight loops over network requests
optionExplanations: Correct. Marking a function async does not create concurrency — awaiting inside a loop serializes the requests exactly like synchronous code. Starting many promises and awaiting them together (with a bound to respect rate limits) overlaps the network waits, which is where all the time goes.

Tempting because 'single-threaded' sounds like the constraint, but network I/O does not occupy the thread — the event loop can hold hundreds of requests in flight concurrently. The serialization comes from the code's await placement, not from a lack of threads.

Timeout is a failure bound, not a performance lever: requests already complete within it, so raising it changes nothing. The accumulated hours come from running 5,000 waits back-to-back, and no per-call setting can overlap them.

Async/await overhead is microseconds against seconds of network latency per call, and synchronous blocking would still serialize every request while also freezing the event loop. This doubles down on the actual problem — sequential waiting — to shave an irrelevant cost.
principle: await-in-a-loop is sequential — concurrency comes from overlapping the promises
relatedConcept: Async syntax enables concurrency but does not grant it: I/O-bound throughput requires structuring code so many requests are in flight at once.
overallExplanation: An async function that awaits each call in a loop is still sequential. Overlapping the requests — Promise.all batches or a bounded pool — is what converts hours of stacked network waits into minutes.

question: A veterinary-clinic chain builds Messages API request bodies by interpolating clinical notes into a JSON string template with f-strings. Requests intermittently fail with 400 errors — always on notes containing quotation marks, newlines, or backslashes. The author proposes regex-escaping those three characters. What should the reviewer require instead?
options: Build the payload as native data structures and let a proper JSON serializer or the SDK produce the wire format, eliminating the escaping problem as a class
Extend the regex to escape all characters that are special in JSON, keeping the string template since it makes the request structure easy to read
Base64-encode every clinical note before insertion so no special characters can reach the JSON layer, decoding on the response side
Add validation that rejects notes containing quotation marks, newlines, or backslashes, asking clinics to rewrite the affected records
optionExplanations: Correct. Hand-assembling JSON by string interpolation is a classic defect generator: any unescaped structural character corrupts the document. Serializers exist to make this a solved problem — construct dicts or objects and serialize, or use the SDK, and the entire failure class disappears.

Tempting because it patches the observed cases, but hand-maintained escaping chases a spec the serializer already implements — control characters, unicode edge cases, nesting. Every gap ships as an intermittent 400, and the 'readable template' remains a latent injection point.

Base64 wrapping makes the payload opaque to the model — Claude would receive encoded gibberish instead of clinical text unless it is decoded first, which reintroduces the original problem. It contorts the data to protect a fragile construction method the serializer makes unnecessary.

Rejecting legitimate clinical content because the client cannot encode it inverts the responsibility: quotation marks and line breaks are normal prose. Asking clinics to rewrite medical records to accommodate a string-template bug is a process cost paid to avoid a one-line code fix.
principle: never build JSON by string interpolation — serialize native data structures
relatedConcept: JSON fluency includes knowing that wire formats come from serializers, not templates; interpolated user text is an encoding bug and an injection risk.
overallExplanation: Escaping bugs are a symptom of hand-built JSON. Constructing payloads as native structures and serializing them — or using the SDK — eliminates the entire failure class rather than patching character by character.

question: A disaster-mapping nonprofit is promoting a volunteer's Claude integration script into its production pipeline. The script currently makes bare API calls with no timeout handling and prints nothing but final results. Which two changes most improve its production readiness? (Choose two.)
options: Add request timeouts and bounded retries with exponential backoff for transient failures such as 429 and overloaded errors
Add structured logging that records each call's request identifier, token usage, latency, and outcome for debugging and monitoring
Wrap the entire pipeline in a broad try/except that swallows all exceptions and continues, so no single failure can ever interrupt a run
Insert a fixed ten-second sleep between all API calls so that no error handling or retry logic is needed anywhere in the script
optionExplanations: Correct. Production network calls need failure discipline: timeouts prevent indefinite hangs, and bounded backoff-retries absorb the transient errors any long-running pipeline will encounter. Without them, one flaky request stalls or kills a run that dozens of responders depend on.

Correct. Observability is what turns a production incident from archaeology into a query: request identifiers correlate failures with provider-side records, and per-call token usage and latency reveal cost drift and degradation before they become outages. Print-nothing scripts are undebuggable at 3 a.m.

Swallowing every exception converts crashes into silent data corruption — the pipeline 'succeeds' while mapping regions with missing or wrong analysis. Resilience means handling anticipated failures deliberately and surfacing the rest loudly, not suppressing all signals of trouble.

A fixed sleep neither prevents nor handles failures — networks still drop, servers still return 5xx, and the script still has no answer for them. It also throttles the pipeline permanently to guard against errors it cannot actually absorb, paying constant latency for zero resilience.
principle: production integrations need failure handling and observability, not hope
relatedConcept: Promoting a script to production means adding timeout/retry discipline for transient failures and structured logging for debugging and monitoring.
overallExplanation: Two things separate a script from a production integration: deliberate failure handling (timeouts, bounded backoff for transient errors) and observability (request ids, usage, latency). Sleeps and swallowed exceptions provide neither.

question: An airline's operations platform has grown Claude calls in roughly thirty places — crew messaging, delay summaries, baggage queries — each call site with its own copy of the model identifier, retry logic, and response parsing. Updating the pinned model last month required thirty coordinated edits and missed two. What refactoring should the staff engineer drive?
options: Consolidate access behind one internal client module that owns model configuration, retries, and parsing, so call sites express intent and cross-cutting changes happen in one place
Keep the thirty independent call sites, since duplication lets each product team tune its own integration without coordinating changes with others
Standardize a project-wide find-and-replace checklist for model updates, making the thirty-edit procedure repeatable instead of ad hoc
Fork the vendor SDK into the monorepo and hardcode the airline's defaults inside the fork so every call site inherits them from the dependency
optionExplanations: Correct. Thirty copies of the same cross-cutting concerns is a textbook abstraction gap: a thin internal wrapper centralizes model pinning, retry policy, logging, and parsing, so the next model migration is one reviewed change instead of a thirty-edit hunt that misses two.

Tempting as team autonomy, but the scenario shows the copies are not intentional variation — they are the same logic drifting apart by accident. Autonomy worth having lives in parameters and options on a shared client, not in thirty divergent implementations of retries.

A checklist institutionalizes the failure mode instead of removing it: the process still requires humans to find every copy, and the last migration missed two even with coordination. Making a bad procedure repeatable is not refactoring; it is documenting the debt.

Forking the SDK buys the worst of both worlds: the team now maintains a diverging copy of vendor code, absorbing every upstream update by hand, to achieve what a thin wrapper module provides without any fork. Defaults belong in your layer, not in patched vendor internals.
principle: centralize cross-cutting integration concerns behind one internal client
relatedConcept: DRY applied to LLM integrations: model config, retries, and parsing are cross-cutting concerns that belong in a shared module, not at every call site.
overallExplanation: When one logical change requires thirty edits, the abstraction is missing. A single internal client module makes model pinning, retries, and parsing one-place changes and turns call sites into expressions of intent.

question: A tax-software firm's unit test suite for its deduction-explainer feature calls the live Claude API on every run. The suite is slow, costs real money on every commit, and fails nondeterministically when responses vary. Developers have started skipping it. How should the team restructure its testing?
options: Mock or stub the API client in unit tests so application logic is verified deterministically and cheaply, and exercise the real model in a separate evaluation or integration suite
Keep the live calls but set temperature to 0 in tests, which makes the model's responses deterministic and therefore reliable enough for unit assertions
Delete the tests that touch the Claude integration, since code paths involving a nondeterministic dependency cannot be meaningfully tested at all
Run the full live suite only before quarterly releases, accepting that commits between releases receive no automated verification of the feature
optionExplanations: Correct. Unit tests verify your code — parsing, prompt assembly, error handling — and a mocked client makes them fast, free, and deterministic. Model behavior itself is real and worth testing, but that belongs in a separately run eval or integration suite, not in the per-commit unit path.

Tempting because low temperature does reduce variance, but it does not guarantee identical outputs, and the suite remains slow and metered — the reasons developers skip it stay intact. Tuning sampling treats a test-architecture problem as a parameter problem.

Nondeterminism in a dependency is a boundary-design problem, not a testability death sentence: mock the boundary and the application logic tests deterministically. Deleting the tests abandons coverage of parsing and error handling that has nothing nondeterministic about it.

Quarterly-only verification means a broken integration can sit unnoticed for months of commits, making the eventual failure archaeology. The fix is making per-commit tests cheap enough to run always, not rationing expensive tests until feedback is useless.
principle: unit-test your logic against a mocked client; test the model in a separate eval suite
relatedConcept: Testing LLM applications splits cleanly: deterministic unit tests with stubbed clients for application code, and dedicated eval runs for model behavior.
overallExplanation: Live API calls do not belong in the per-commit unit path. Stub the client to test application logic deterministically, and give real model behavior its own evaluation suite with its own cadence.

question: A construction project-management SaaS gives Claude an update_task tool whose 'status' parameter is a free-form string. In production, Claude populates it with values like 'nearly finished' and 'blocked on permits', which the task service rejects. The prompt already lists the valid statuses. What schema change fixes this properly?
options: Constrain the parameter in the tool's JSON Schema — an enum of the valid status values, marked required, with a description of when each applies
Add a post-processing layer that fuzzy-matches whatever string Claude produces to the nearest official status before calling the task service
Strengthen the system prompt with capitalized warnings that only the listed statuses may ever be used in the status field
Have the tool return an error to Claude on invalid statuses and rely on it retrying until it happens to produce an accepted value
optionExplanations: Correct. Schema design is the enforcement point for tool inputs: an enum tells the model the complete legal value set in the contract it fills against, and required plus per-value description guidance makes correct population the path of least resistance. Prose lists are advice; schema constraints are structure.

Fuzzy-matching launders bad values instead of preventing them — 'blocked on permits' silently becomes some official status the mapper guesses, and a wrong guess corrupts project data invisibly. It builds permanent infrastructure to compensate for a one-line schema omission.

The prompt already lists the statuses and the model still improvises, because free-form strings invite natural language. Louder prose remains probabilistic guidance; the parameter's schema is where the value set becomes part of the structural contract the model fills.

Error-driven retry works as a backstop, but as the primary mechanism it spends extra round-trips and tokens rediscovering, per call, a value set that could be declared once in the schema. Design the contract to prevent the error, then keep validation as defense in depth.
principle: encode legal values in the tool schema — enums constrain what prompts merely suggest
relatedConcept: Tool schema design: enums, required fields, types, and precise parameter descriptions are how applications make model tool calls conform.
overallExplanation: When a tool parameter has a closed value set, put the set in the schema as an enum. Prose lists in prompts are suggestions; the JSON Schema is the contract the model actually fills against.

question: At a biotech research lab, scientists have been individually installing whatever community plugins and MCP servers they find into the shared Claude environment. Sessions now show duplicate and conflicting tool names, and an audit found one unvetted server with broad filesystem access to shared drives. How should the platform team manage plugins going forward?
options: Treat plugins as managed dependencies: maintain a vetted, version-controlled set in shared configuration, and review new additions for capability and access before adoption
Ban plugins and MCP servers outright, since community-authored extensions can never be made safe enough for a research environment handling shared data
Let each scientist continue managing a personal plugin list, but circulate a wiki page of known conflicts so people can avoid problematic combinations
Keep installations open but rename conflicting tools by hand whenever a collision is noticed in a session
optionExplanations: Correct. Plugin management is a design responsibility: each plugin extends what the assistant can see and do, so the set must be curated like any dependency — vetted for capabilities and access, version-controlled in shared configuration, and changed through review rather than ad hoc installs.

A blanket ban forfeits the ecosystem's genuine value and usually drives shadow installs that are harder to audit than a sanctioned path. The audit finding argues for governance — vetting, least-privilege review, a managed set — not for prohibition of the entire mechanism.

A conflicts wiki documents the chaos without reducing it: the unvetted filesystem-access server remains installed, versions still drift per person, and nothing prevents the next risky addition. Awareness of a problem is not a control on it.

Hand-renaming collisions treats the visible symptom while the governance gap — anyone installing anything, with any access level — continues generating both conflicts and security exposure. It is per-incident cleanup standing in for dependency management.
principle: plugins extend capability and access — curate them as managed, reviewed dependencies
relatedConcept: Plugin management in Claude application design: a vetted, version-controlled plugin set with capability review, not ad hoc per-user installs.
overallExplanation: Every plugin changes the assistant's capability surface and access footprint. Managing them as vetted, version-controlled dependencies — with review before adoption — is the design practice that prevents both tool conflicts and unvetted access.

question: A supply-chain SaaS team maintains a thorough CLAUDE.md that keeps Claude Code sessions following their conventions perfectly. They assumed those conventions would also govern their product's Messages API integration, but the production assistant ignores them entirely. Which two statements correctly describe the situation? (Choose two.)
options: CLAUDE.md is a Claude Code mechanism — it is read into coding sessions and has no effect on requests the product sends to the Messages API
For the API integration, equivalent guidance must be supplied explicitly, typically as part of the system prompt the application sends with its requests
Uploading the CLAUDE.md file in the developer console binds it account-wide, applying its conventions to all API traffic under those keys
The client SDK automatically discovers a CLAUDE.md in the process's working directory and prepends it to outgoing requests at runtime
optionExplanations: Correct. CLAUDE.md belongs to the Claude Code interface: the tool loads it as session context for coding work. The Messages API knows nothing of it — an API request contains exactly what the application sends, and no file on the developers' machines participates.

Correct. Each interface supplies its own instruction plumbing, and the raw API's is explicit: whatever conventions should govern the production assistant must travel in the request, normally in the system prompt, shipped and versioned as part of the application.

No console mechanism binds a CLAUDE.md to an account or its API keys — this imagines Claude Code's file convention grafted onto the API as account-level configuration. API behavior is controlled per request by request content, not by uploaded convention files.

The SDK is a thin client for the API; it does not scan the filesystem for instruction files or silently modify payloads. Automatic CLAUDE.md discovery is a Claude Code behavior, and expecting it from the SDK confuses the two layers.
principle: CLAUDE.md configures Claude Code sessions — API requests carry only what you send
relatedConcept: How Claude interprets instructions differs by interface: Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md; the Messages API receives instructions only through the request itself.
overallExplanation: Instruction mechanisms are interface-specific. CLAUDE.md shapes Claude Code sessions, not API traffic; a production API integration must carry its conventions explicitly in its own system prompt.

question: A municipal water utility's assistant answers account and outage questions well, but auditors found it also confidently answers billing-dispute and legal-liability questions it was never designed for — sometimes incorrectly, in a regulated domain. The model tier and prompt quality are otherwise fine. What design element is missing?
options: Explicit scope boundaries with an escalation path: define the topics the assistant must decline or hand off, instruct and enforce that behavior, and route those requests to staff
A more capable model tier, so that answers to billing-dispute and liability questions become accurate enough to keep handling them in the assistant
A standard disclaimer footer appended to every response stating that answers are informational and should not be relied upon for disputes
A lower temperature setting, which reduces the model's tendency to produce incorrect answers on topics outside its designed coverage
optionExplanations: Correct. Applications need designed edges: an explicit statement of what is in and out of scope, prompt instructions that make the assistant decline or redirect out-of-scope topics, and a working handoff so users reach humans. Without that boundary, the model helpfully answers whatever arrives.

Tempting as a quality fix, but it expands the assistant's de facto mandate instead of defining it — the utility never decided the assistant should adjudicate disputes or discuss liability. In a regulated domain, some topics belong with staff regardless of how accurate the model becomes.

A blanket disclaimer neither prevents the wrong answers nor absolves them; users act on confident responses whatever the footer says, and regulators judge the behavior, not the boilerplate. It decorates the failure rather than designing the boundary that prevents it.

Temperature adjusts sampling variability, not topical scope: at any setting the model still attempts out-of-scope questions, just with steadier wording. The failure is that these questions are answered at all, which only a designed scope-and-escalation policy addresses.
principle: design the edges: declared scope, refusal behavior, and a human handoff path
relatedConcept: Claude application design includes deciding what the assistant must not answer and engineering the decline-and-escalate behavior for those cases.
overallExplanation: An assistant's scope is a design artifact, not an emergent property. Declaring out-of-scope topics, instructing refusal, and routing users to staff is what keeps a helpful model from freelancing in regulated territory.

question: A community-forum platform uses Claude to write moderation summaries that quote user posts, and the dashboard renders these summaries directly as HTML. A security reviewer notes that a hostile user could craft a post whose content survives into the summary as executable markup. What rendering design should the team adopt?
options: Treat model output as untrusted for rendering — escape or sanitize it before inserting into the page, exactly as the platform would with user-derived content
Add a system prompt instruction requiring Claude to emit only safe, well-formed HTML free of scripts or event handlers in every summary
Rely on the model's safety training, since an aligned model will not reproduce malicious markup from a user post into its summary
Sanitize user posts before they reach the model, which makes the summary output safe to render without any further processing
optionExplanations: Correct. Model output that incorporates user content is user-derived content: the standard web-security posture — escape by default, sanitize where rich markup is needed — must apply at the rendering boundary. The defense belongs in code the attacker cannot influence, not in model behavior.

A prompt instruction is probabilistic guidance, not a security control: adversarial post content is specifically crafted to survive such instructions, and one miss is one stored-XSS incident. Instructions can reduce accidents; the rendering layer must still assume output is unsafe.

Safety training targets harmful content, not HTML injection semantics — a model can faithfully quote a post containing markup without recognizing it as an attack on the downstream renderer. Alignment is not a sanitizer, and treating it as one leaves the XSS path open.

Input sanitization helps, but it is insufficient alone: transformations by the model can reassemble or unescape dangerous sequences, and non-post inputs also flow into summaries. Output encoding at the render boundary is the control that holds regardless of what happened upstream.
principle: render model output as untrusted content — escape and sanitize at the boundary
relatedConcept: Content boundaries run in both directions: LLM output that embeds user content must pass the same rendering defenses as raw user input.
overallExplanation: Summaries that quote users are user-derived content wearing the model's voice. Escaping and sanitizing model output at the rendering boundary is the enforceable control; prompts and alignment are not security layers.

question: An e-commerce marketplace has Claude generate order-summary emails, and the prompt also asks it to compute each order's refund total from the line items. Audits show the prose is excellent but the arithmetic is occasionally wrong — off by small amounts on long orders. How should the team divide this work?
options: Compute the refund total deterministically in application code and pass the finished figure into the prompt, using Claude only for the language work it excels at
Add several worked examples of refund arithmetic to the prompt, since multi-shot demonstrations reliably correct a model's calculation errors
Enable extended thinking on every email generation so the model has enough reasoning capacity to get the arithmetic consistently right
Generate each email twice and compare the two computed totals, sending the email only when both runs independently agree on the amount
optionExplanations: Correct. Application design assigns each layer what it does best: arithmetic is deterministic and belongs in code, where it is exact, testable, and free. The model receives the computed figure and does the genuinely linguistic work — a division of labor that removes the error class entirely.

Tempting because examples improve many behaviors, but token-by-token generation is not a calculator: demonstrations reduce arithmetic mistakes without eliminating them, and money is a domain where 'usually right' is a defect. No prompt makes probabilistic arithmetic exact.

Extended thinking improves multi-step reasoning, and would likely raise accuracy at real latency and token cost — but it still cannot guarantee correctness on a task code performs perfectly for free. Paying for probabilistic arithmetic when exact arithmetic is one line of code is a design error.

Agreement between two probabilistic runs is not proof of correctness — both can share the same systematic slip — and disagreement leaves the pipeline stuck in retries. It doubles cost to approximate a guarantee that a single line of application code provides outright.
principle: deterministic computation belongs in code; the model does the language work
relatedConcept: A core Claude application design decision is the seam between code and model: calculations, lookups, and validation in code; understanding and generation in the model.
overallExplanation: Do not buy probabilistic arithmetic when exact arithmetic is free. Computing totals in code and handing the model finished figures assigns each layer its strength and eliminates the error class.

question: A car-rental platform is designing a support chat where customers can leave and resume conversations across visits and devices. The team is deciding how conversation state should be handled. Which two design decisions are correct? (Choose two.)
options: Key stored transcripts to the authenticated customer and ensure a resumed session can never replay another customer's conversation into the context
Define a retention and expiry policy for stored conversation data, since transcripts accumulate personal details like addresses and booking history
Pass a conversation_id parameter on each request so the Messages API stores and recalls the conversation history server-side between visits
Cache completed conversations in a shared store keyed by question text, so similar questions from other customers can reuse existing transcripts as context
optionExplanations: Correct. Persistence makes session hygiene an authorization problem: history is loaded by the application, so the application must guarantee the transcript it replays belongs to the authenticated customer. A keying or lookup bug here is a direct cross-customer data leak into the model's context.

Correct. Stored transcripts are a personal-data store and must be designed as one: retention limits, expiry, and deletion honor both privacy obligations and users' reasonable expectations. Conversation state that lives forever is a liability accumulating silently.

The Messages API offers no conversation_id or server-side conversation storage — it is stateless, and each request carries its own history. Designing around this imagined mechanism would leave the resume feature unbuilt and misplace responsibility for state the application must own.

Reusing one customer's transcript as context for another is a data leak by design — names, bookings, and addresses would flow between accounts through 'similar' questions. Whatever caching the platform adds must never blend conversational state across customers.
principle: the application owns conversation state — scope it per user and give it a lifecycle
relatedConcept: Session hygiene for persistent chat: transcripts are per-user personal data requiring strict scoping on replay and a deliberate retention policy.
overallExplanation: Cross-visit chat means the application stores and replays state, which raises two design duties: strict per-customer scoping so contexts never mix, and a retention policy because transcripts are accumulating personal data.

question: A railway operator's assistant answers signalling questions by concatenating its instructions, excerpts from three different equipment manuals, and the operator's question into one undifferentiated block of text. In testing, the model regularly attributes procedures from one manual to equipment covered by another. What prompt-structure change addresses this?
options: Delimit each component structurally — for example wrap each manual excerpt in labeled tags carrying its source, and separate instructions and the question into their own marked sections
Limit every request to a single manual excerpt, accepting that questions spanning equipment from multiple manuals can no longer be answered
Ask the model to begin each answer by listing which manuals it received, so operators can spot attribution mistakes before acting on a procedure
Raise max_tokens so longer answers give the model room to discuss each manual separately instead of blending them together
optionExplanations: Correct. When sources arrive as one undifferentiated blob, the model has no structural signal for where one document ends and another begins — conflation is the predictable result. Labeled delimiters (such as XML-style tags with source metadata) make document boundaries and roles explicit, which is precisely what attribution requires.

Tempting because it eliminates cross-document confusion by construction, but it amputates the capability instead of fixing the prompt: cross-manual questions are real operator needs. Structure lets multiple sources coexist distinguishably; restriction just narrows the product.

An inventory preamble adds a human-detectable symptom report while leaving the cause — indistinguishable sources — fully intact. The model can list three manuals correctly and still misattribute procedures among them; safety-critical attribution should be engineered, not eyeballed.

The failure is conflation, not compression: the model mixes sources because it cannot tell them apart, not because it lacks room to treat them separately. A longer budget produces longer answers with the same misattributions.
principle: delimit and label every content source so document boundaries are structural, not inferred
relatedConcept: Content boundaries in prompt construction: instructions, each document, and the question belong in clearly labeled sections the model can tell apart.
overallExplanation: Models attribute reliably only when sources are structurally distinguishable. Wrapping each document in labeled delimiters and separating instructions from data turns an undifferentiated blob into a prompt the model can navigate.

question: A smart-home company's support summarizer degraded sharply yesterday. The team iterates quickly, editing the production prompt in place several times a week, and now cannot determine which of the recent edits caused the regression or reconstruct what the prompt said when the bad outputs were generated. What configuration practice was missing?
options: Prompt versioning with traceability: treat each prompt revision as an identified, versioned artifact and record which version produced each response, enabling diagnosis and rollback
A rule that only the most senior engineer may edit the production prompt, reducing the number of people who could have introduced the regression
A manually maintained changelog document where engineers are asked to note the date and reason each time they adjust the prompt's wording
An instruction appended to the prompt asking Claude to flag in its output whenever its own behavior differs from previous responses
optionExplanations: Correct. Prompt versioning closes the loop the team is missing: every revision gets an identity, and every response records which version generated it. Yesterday's outputs then point to an exact prompt state — diffable against its predecessor and revertible in one step — instead of a guess.

Restricting editors shrinks the suspect list without creating any evidence: the senior engineer's in-place edits would be exactly as unreconstructable. The gap is that prompt states and outputs are not linked, and no author policy produces that linkage.

A voluntary changelog decays precisely when it matters — under rapid iteration, entries get skipped, and nothing ties a logged edit to the responses it produced. Versioning must be enforced by the workflow and joined to output records, not remembered as a courtesy.

The model has no memory of previous responses to compare against and cannot audit its own configuration history; such self-reports would be confabulation. Change tracking is an engineering-system responsibility that cannot be delegated to the artifact being tracked.
principle: version every prompt revision and record which version produced each output
relatedConcept: Prompt versioning is configuration management: identified prompt artifacts plus response-level version logging give regressions a diffable, revertible cause.
overallExplanation: Fast prompt iteration is safe only with versioned artifacts and output traceability. When each response records the prompt version that produced it, a regression becomes a diff and a rollback instead of a mystery.

question: An online grocery's services hardcode Claude model identifiers and request parameters in source across a dozen repositories. When a new model version was announced, the team could not trial it in staging without code changes and redeploys everywhere, so the upgrade evaluation stalled for a quarter. What change unblocks this properly?
options: Externalize model identifiers and parameters into per-environment configuration, so staging can pin a candidate version for validation while production stays on the current pin
Switch every service to the provider's latest-model alias so new versions arrive automatically and no environment ever needs a coordinated upgrade
Keep the hardcoded identifiers but add a code comment beside each one noting the date it was last reviewed and who approved the choice
Consolidate on a single shared constant for the model identifier that all environments import, ensuring staging and production always run identical values
optionExplanations: Correct. Model choice is configuration, not code: externalizing it per environment lets staging point at a candidate version for evaluation while production remains pinned, turning upgrades into a config change plus validation instead of a dozen coordinated redeploys.

Tempting as the zero-effort path, but a latest alias means production model behavior changes on the provider's schedule, untested — the classic silent-upgrade failure. The team's problem is friction in deliberate upgrades; the fix cannot be surrendering deliberateness.

Comments document the hardcoding without curing it: trialing a version still requires editing source and redeploying every service, so the quarterly stall recurs at the next release. Review metadata is not a substitute for moving the value into configuration.

A shared constant deduplicates the value but enforces the exact constraint that caused the stall — staging cannot diverge to evaluate a candidate while production holds. Environments need independently settable configuration, not a single value welded across both.
principle: model identifiers are per-environment configuration, not source-code constants
relatedConcept: Configuration management enables safe model upgrades: staging pins a candidate for validation while production's pin moves only after evals pass.
overallExplanation: Upgrades stall when model choice lives in code. Per-environment configuration lets staging evaluate a candidate version while production stays pinned, making adoption a validated config change rather than a mass redeploy.

question: A CAD-software firm's development workflow depends on Claude Code with several MCP-server plugins. After one plugin auto-updated and changed its tool behavior, half the team's automation broke while the other half — on older versions — was fine. Which two practices should the team adopt? (Choose two.)
options: Pin plugin and MCP-server versions, adopting updates deliberately after testing, since plugin changes alter the tool surface the team's automation depends on
Declare the required plugin set and versions in shared, version-controlled project configuration so every developer and CI environment resolves the same dependencies
Configure all plugins to auto-update silently to the latest release, ensuring version drift between teammates can never occur again
Have each developer curate a personal plugin list independently, so a bad update affects only the individuals who happened to install it
optionExplanations: Correct. The incident is a dependency-management failure: an unpinned plugin changed underneath workflows that depended on its behavior. Pinning versions and promoting updates through testing applies the same discipline the team already uses for libraries to its Claude tooling.

Correct. A shared, version-controlled declaration of the plugin set makes environments reproducible: every developer and CI run resolves identical plugins at identical versions, and changes to the set arrive through reviewed commits rather than word of mouth.

Universal silent auto-update does end drift — by making every machine break simultaneously when the next behavioral change ships, with no tested rollback point. It maximizes exposure to exactly the failure that just occurred in exchange for consistency of the untested.

Personal plugin lists institutionalize the half-broken-half-fine split from the incident: environments diverge permanently, automation works only on some machines, and debugging starts with archaeology of each individual's setup. Blast-radius thinking cannot justify irreproducibility.
principle: plugins are dependencies: pin versions and declare them in shared configuration
relatedConcept: Plugin dependencies in Claude system configuration deserve lockfile discipline — pinned versions, shared declaration, tested upgrades.
overallExplanation: Treat Claude tooling plugins like any dependency: pinned versions upgraded deliberately after testing, declared in shared version-controlled configuration so every environment resolves the same set.

question: At a robotics startup, an engineer committed his personal preferences — his favorite permission grants and local tool paths — into the project's shared settings.json in the repository. Teammates' Claude Code sessions promptly broke on machines where those paths do not exist. How should the team organize its settings?
options: Keep team-wide policy in the shared project settings.json under version control, and put personal preferences and machine-specific values in settings.local.json, which is not committed
Move all settings to each developer's user-level configuration so the repository carries no settings file and no commit can affect anyone else's sessions
Add a second committed settings file per developer to the repository, named after each engineer, so everyone's personal configuration is versioned alongside the code
Stop using settings files for the project and rely on verbal team agreements about which permissions and tools everyone should configure by hand
optionExplanations: Correct. The settings hierarchy exists for exactly this split: the project's shared settings.json carries team policy every clone should get, while settings.local.json holds personal, machine-specific overrides and stays out of version control. Each concern lives at the layer scoped to it.

Retreating entirely to user-level configuration throws out shared policy: nothing in the repo establishes the team's common permissions and conventions, so every machine drifts and onboarding becomes manual setup folklore. The fix is layering, not abandonment of the shared layer.

Per-developer committed files clutter the repository with configuration that is meaningless off its owner's machine and invite the same breakage whenever tooling reads the wrong one. Machine-specific values are deliberately excluded from version control by the local-settings layer.

Verbal agreements are configuration without enforcement or history — the precise gap settings files close. Hand-configured environments drift immediately, and the team loses the reviewable, reproducible baseline a committed project settings file provides.
principle: shared policy in committed project settings; personal overrides in uncommitted local settings
relatedConcept: The settings.json hierarchy separates team-wide, version-controlled configuration from per-developer settings.local.json overrides.
overallExplanation: Settings layering solves the conflict: the committed project settings.json defines team policy for every clone, while personal and machine-specific values live in the uncommitted settings.local.json.
